title: Liliom
author: Ferenc Molnár
note: Benjamin F. Glazer’s 1921 Theatre Guild English — carousel barker from prologue to beyond the grave. Opens at THE PROLOGUE.

scenes.title: THE PROLOGUE
scenes.reentry: An amusement park on the outskirts of Budapest on a late afternoon in Spring.

scenes.title: Scene — lonely park
scenes.reentry: SCENE--_A lonely place in the park, half hidden by trees and shrubbery.

breaths.text: An amusement park on the outskirts of Budapest on a late afternoon in Spring.
Barkers stand before the booths of the sideshows haranguing the passing crowd.
The strident music of a calliope is heard; laughter, shouts, the scuffle of feet, the signal bells of merry-go-round.
The merry-go-round is at Center.
LILIOM stands at the entrance, a cigarette in his mouth, coaxing the people in.
The girls regard him with idolizing glances and screech with pleasure as he playfully pushes them through entrance.

Now and then some girl's escort resents the familiarity, whereupon LILIOM'S demeanor becomes ugly and menacing, and the cowed escort slinks through the entrance behind his girl or contents himself with a muttered resentful comment.
One girl hands LILIOM a red carnation; he rewards her with a bow and a smile.
When the soldier who accompanies her protests, LILIOM cows him with a fierce glance and a threatening gesture.
MARIE and JULIE come out of the crowd and LILIOM favors them with particular notice as they pass into the merry-go-round.
MRS. MUSKAT comes out of the merry-go-round, bringing LILIOM coffee and rolls.
LILIOM mounts the barker's stand at the entrance, where he is elevated over everyone on the stage.
Here he begins his harangue.
Everybody turns toward him.
The other booths are gradually deserted.
The tumult makes it impossible for the audience to hear what he is saying, but every now and then some witticism of his provokes a storm of laughter which is audible above the din.
Many people enter the merry-go-round.
Here and there one catches a phrase "Room for one more on the zebra's back," "Which of you ladies?"
"Ten heller for adults, five for children," "Step right up"---It is growing darker.
A lamplighter crosses the stage, and begins unperturbedly lighting the colored gas-lamps.
The whistle of a distant locomotive is heard.
Suddenly the tumult ceases, the lights go out, and the curtain falls in darkness.
SCENE--_A lonely place in the park, half hidden by trees and shrubbery.
Under a flowering acacia tree stands a painted wooden bench.
From the distance, faintly, comes the tumult of the amusement park.
It is the sunset of the same day._
_When the curtain rises the stage is empty._
_MARIE enters quickly, pauses at center, and looks back._
Marie: Julie, Julie!
Marie: [_There is no answer._] Do you hear me, Julie?
Marie: Let her be!
Marie: Come on.
Marie: Let her be.
Marie: [_Starts to go back._] [_JULIE enters, looks back angrily._] JULIE Did you ever hear of such a thing?
Marie: What's the matter with the woman anyway?
[_Looking back again._]
Marie: Here she comes again.
Julie: Let her come.
Julie: I didn't do anything to her.
Julie: All of a sudden she comes up to me and begins to raise a row.
Marie: Here she is.
Marie: Come on, let's run.
Marie: [_Tries to urge her off._] JULIE Run?
Marie: I should say not.
Marie: What would I want to run for?
Marie: I'm not afraid of her.
Marie: Oh, come on.
Marie: She'll only start a fight.
Julie: I'm going to stay right here.
Julie: Let her _start_ a fight.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT [_Entering._] What do you want to run away for?
Julie: [_To JULIE._] Don't worry.
Julie: I won't eat you.
Julie: But there's one thing I want to tell you, my dear.
Julie: Don't let me catch you in my carousel again.
Julie: I stand for a whole lot, I have to in my business.
Julie: It makes no difference to me whether my customers are ladies or the likes of you--as long as they pay their money.
Julie: But when a girl misbehaves herself on my carousel--out she goes.
Julie: Do you understand?
Julie: Are you talking to me?
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Yes, you!
Julie: You--chamber-maid, you!
Julie: In my carousel----
Julie: Who did anything in your old carousel?
Julie: I paid my fare and took my seat and never said a word, except to my friend here.
Marie: No, she never opened her mouth.
Marie: Liliom came over to her of his own accord.
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT It's all the same.
Marie: I'm not going to get in trouble with the police, and lose my license on account of you--you shabby kitchen maid!
Julie: Shabby yourself.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT You stay out of my carousel!
Julie: Letting my barker fool with you!
Julie: Aren't you ashamed of yourself?
Julie: What?
Julie: What did you say?
Julie: I suppose you think I have no eyes in my head.
Julie: I see everything that goes on in my carousel.
Julie: During the whole ride she let Liliom fool with her--the shameless hussy!
Julie: He did not fool with me!
Julie: I don't let any man fool with me!
Julie: He leaned against you all through the ride!
Julie: He leaned against the panther.
Julie: He always leans against something, doesn't he?
Julie: Everybody leans where he wants.
Julie: I couldn't tell him not to lean, if he always leans, could I?
Julie: But he didn't lay a hand on me.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Oh, didn't he?
Julie: And I suppose he didn't put his hand around your waist, either?
Marie: And if he did?
Marie: What of it?
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT You hold your tongue!
Marie: No one's asking you--just you keep out of it.
Julie: He put his arm around my waist--just the same as he does to all the girls.
Julie: He always does that.
Julie: I'll teach him not to do it any more, my dear.
Julie: No carryings on in my carousel!
